title: Destroying Asteroids
statement:
A planet starts with mass `mass`, and `asteroids[i]` is the mass of the `i`-th asteroid. You may make the planet hit the asteroids one at a time, in whatever order you choose.

When the planet hits an asteroid whose mass is at most the planet's current mass, the asteroid is destroyed and its mass is added to the planet. When the asteroid is heavier than the planet, the planet is destroyed instead.

Return `true` if some order lets the planet destroy every asteroid, and `false` otherwise.
notes:
## Intuition

The planet only ever grows, so destroying an asteroid early never makes a later one harder. The question is which one to hit next. The lightest remaining asteroid is the safest choice: if even it is too heavy, every other one is too, and the planet is doomed whatever order we pick. If it is edible, eating it only adds mass.

So sorting the asteroids by mass and hitting them in that order is optimal. (Trying every order would be factorial; repeatedly scanning for any edible asteroid works but is quadratic.)

## Approach

1. Sort `asteroids` in increasing order.
2. Set `planet` to `mass`.
3. Walk the sorted list. If an `asteroid` is heavier than `planet`, return `false`.
4. Otherwise add its mass to `planet` and continue.
5. If the loop finishes, every asteroid was destroyed: return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

`mass = 10`, sorted `asteroids = [3,5,9,19,21]`. The planet goes `10 → 13 → 18 → 27`; then `19 <= 27` gives `46`, and `21 <= 46` gives `67`. No asteroid was too heavy, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sort; the scan is O(n).
- Space: O(1) beyond the sort.

## Pitfalls

- The comparison is "at most": an asteroid of exactly the planet's mass is destroyed, so test `asteroid > planet`.
- The planet's mass can reach about 10^10, which overflows a 32-bit `int` in Java or C; use a 64-bit type (or stop once it passes 10^5).
- Sorting with the default JavaScript `sort()` compares as strings; pass `(a, b) => a - b`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `planet` | the planet's current mass |
| `asteroid` | the asteroid being hit next, in sorted order |

narration.2: Sort the asteroids so the lightest, safest one always comes next.
narration.3: The planet starts with its original mass.
narration.4: Hit the asteroids from lightest to heaviest.
narration.5: If even the lightest remaining asteroid is heavier than the planet, all the rest are too.
narration.6: So no order can work: report failure.
narration.8: The asteroid is destroyed and its mass joins the planet.
narration.10: Every asteroid was destroyed, so the answer is true.
